objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII settlement with the UK by June so the Council can vote on the implementing act on schedule, avoiding the reputational and legal friction of an unagreed modification.
Secure UK acquiescence to the TRQ architecture (volume, allocation, administration) at terms the Commission can defend to both steel-producing and steel-consuming member states.
Prevent a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute or coordinated disapplication of FTA commitments — this is my red line for escalation and the worst realistic outcome.
Preserve the working relationship with the UK Mission across the wider Goods file and the EU's standing as a reliable negotiating partner in Geneva.
Keep the outcome compatible with the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims, avoiding concessions to the UK that blow up the arithmetic of those separate tracks.
Where possible, lock in stability: a review clause, circumvention disciplines, and clarity on how the settlement interacts with the TCA and the UK's own steel measure.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a signed Article XXVIII settlement by round four (or earlier) that the Council can adopt: a TRQ with allocation and administration arrangements the UK accepts, an out-of-quota rate and duration the Commission can sell to member states, no FTA dispute involving the UK, and no collapse of the parallel claims. Partial success is a settlement that requires modest compensation on other lines but leaves the Geneva relationship intact. Failure is no settlement — the EU proceeds unilaterally on 50%/400kt/FCFS terms, the UK withdraws substantially equivalent concessions against EU steel exports (which are 3.6 million tonnes into the UK market), and worse, the UK joins Japan and Korea in an FTA dispute. Even a 'successful' unilateral modification would be a strategic failure if it triggers that cascade.
declaration.approach: Open with momentum: table something concrete and slightly better than the notified position early — most plausibly a move on allocation method (signalling openness to country-specific shares or licensing rather than pure FCFS) — because the UK cares less about headline volume than about guaranteed, predictable access for its concentrated product mix. Probe for the UK's real priority ordering: volume vs. allocation certainty vs. product carve-outs vs. the FTA disapplication clause. The FTA disapplication provision is my most valuable and most dangerous card: it is what provokes the joint dispute, so I should treat flexibility there (e.g., grandfathering TCA preferences within the quota, or exempting EEA-equivalent treatment) as the big concession to trade against UK acceptance of the core TRQ. Use the symmetry of the two measures — the UK has its own Article XXVIII process and EU exporters hold country-specific quotas under the UK safeguard — to frame a package: EU accommodation on allocation/FTA treatment in exchange for UK accommodation on EU country-specific quota treatment in its measure. Be honest within the room that the modification will proceed regardless; this is true and it concentrates minds, but deliver it without menace. Report candidly to Brussels each round, flagging the dispute risk as the reason to spend real concessions rather than pocket a cheap 'win'. Never let the UK believe a delay past June is costless for the EU; never let Brussels believe the UK will fold under the 400kt/FCFS default.

parties.who: UK Geneva counterpart (UK Mission to the WTO)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access for UK steel into the EU — higher TRQ volume, country-specific allocation or licensing to guarantee UK share (they know a global FCFS 400kt quota against 2.4mt of exports is near-worthless), carve-outs for the specific product lines UK mills concentrate in, reversal or softening of the FTA disapplication clause, and linkage to favourable treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel measure. They will also test whether the June deadline makes the EU desperate.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically defensible outcome for a small number of high-employment steel sites; they cannot accept a settlement that looks like capitulation. Ministerial clearance means they need either a big quota share, product carve-outs, or visible compensation wins. They may be tempted by the Japan/Korea joint dispute as leverage, or as a fallback if talks fail.

A concluded process by June, protection of the permanent steel regime's integrity, no precedent that unravels the FTA disapplication policy wholesale, and a compensation bill small enough to pass the Council with both producing and consuming member states on board. They have given no settlement figure, so they will want options with clear costings.

parties.who: Council / member states (via the Trade Policy Committee)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Steel-producing states (Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Benelux, Nordics) want a tight quota and high out-of-quota rate; steel-consuming manufacturing states want more import access and dislike compensation paid on other lines. This split constrains how much volume I can offer.

Equivalent or better treatment than anything the UK gets — any country-specific share granted to the UK sets a benchmark for their claims. Korea and Japan additionally want the FTA disapplication clause gone or neutered, and are reportedly courting the UK into a joint dispute.

parties.who: EU steel industry and EU downstream users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Industry wants the 50% wall and a small quota; downstream users (automotive, construction, machinery) want quota volume and administrable licensing rather than FCFS chaos. Their pressure reaches me only via Brussels, but shapes the mandate's elasticity.

objectives: Secure an Article XXVIII agreement with the UK before the June Council vote, so the implementing legislation proceeds on schedule and the import regime gains permanent legal footing.

Preserve the core operation of the regime: a materially restrictive bound rate, a quota that significantly reduces UK duty-free access relative to the 2.4 million tonnes they currently ship, and the ability to disapply FTA tariff reductions for non-EEA partners including the UK.

Keep total EU concessions across all claimants (UK, Turkey, Korea, India, Japan) within a defensible envelope — anything conceded to the UK sets a benchmark for larger suppliers, so UK-specific generosity must be justified by its principal supplying interest and the TCA relationship, not given away as precedent.
Avoid UK retaliation and avoid destabilising the EU-UK TCA relationship at a moment when the US is already threatening tariff retaliation against the EU.

Manage member state tensions: steel-producing member states want maximum restriction; steel-consuming manufacturers want continued access. The deal must be sellable to the Trade Policy Committee and Council.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a signed Article XXVIII settlement within four rounds that the Council can approve in June: the regime enters into force on time, UK duty-free access is cut substantially (ideally to well under half their current volumes, whether through quota volume, allocation method, or the out-of-quota rate), and the EU gives away no more than a modest, defensible package — ideally concessions structured as preferential treatment for the UK within the regime (a country-specific quota share or carve-outs on product lines where the UK dominates) rather than compensation on unrelated tariff lines that other claimants could cite. Failure is: no settlement (process slips past June, regime delayed, US pressure compounds), or a settlement that concedes so much UK access that Turkey and Korea demand equivalent treatment and the regime's restrictive effect is hollowed out. A deal that is technically agreed but politically unsellable to the Council is also failure.
declaration.approach: Move early and visibly, as instructed — momentum pays. In Round 1, make a concrete, time-boxed opening offer that improves on the notified position in ways that cost me little: signal willingness to discuss a modest increase in quota volume, a country-specific allocation for the UK (which actually serves EU administration interests better than first-come first-served, and lets me control the number), and a review clause (cheap to give, binds me to nothing). Hold firm on the 50% out-of-quota rate and on disapplying FTA preferences — those are the regime's teeth. Use the UK's leverage asymmetry honestly but without overt threats: my analysts say no-deal hurts them far more than us, and they know it, but I should never say so crudely; instead frame everything as 'an agreed outcome protects your industry better than confrontation.' Steer the UK toward asking for things inside the regime (quota share, administration method, product carve-outs) rather than compensation elsewhere in the schedule, because in-regime concessions are controllable, reviewable, and less precedent-setting. Reserve the preferential FTA-partner pool idea as a late-round sweetener only if needed — it is undercooked internally and risks objections from other partners if the UK takes a large share. Keep every offer within the mandate and flag anything that would need Council sign-off early, so I never promise what I cannot deliver. Monitor coordination risk: the UK's own Article XXVIII process and its steel measure (where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas) gives them a hostage — I should expect linkage attempts and be ready to discuss reciprocal treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure as a genuine trade, since that costs the regime nothing.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum duty-free access: highest possible TRQ volume, a UK-specific country allocation sized to their historic trade (~2.4Mt), a lower out-of-quota rate, carve-outs for the product lines where they are concentrated, retention of TCA preferences (i.e., resisting the FTA-disapplication clause), and possibly linkage to treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure. They will press urgency because no-deal devastates their industry.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / Ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically defensible deal that protects the handful of steel sites and their local employment. They need to be able to announce a number — tonnes of secured access — so they will prioritise quota volume and country-specific allocation over abstract legal points, but they cannot be seen to accept the FTA-disapplication clause without something visible in return.

Split: steel-producing member states want minimal concessions and maximum import reduction; manufacturing member states want supply security and low input costs. Collectively they want the file concluded in June without a fight with the UK or a precedent that unravels the regime when Turkey and Korea come to the table.

The tightest possible regime: low quota, high out-of-quota rate, no FTA carve-outs, strong anti-circumvention provisions. They will lobby member states against any generosity to the UK and will be vocal if the deal looks soft.

parties.who: EU downstream steel users (automotive, construction, manufacturing)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Adequate import volumes at reasonable prices; they are quietly sympathetic to a larger TRQ and licensing-based administration that gives supply predictability, but they have less political weight than producers on this file.

Not at this table, but watching it. Any UK-specific deal — especially volume and country allocation — will be cited as the benchmark in their own negotiations. Turkey and Korea ship more than the UK and will demand at least equivalent per-tonne treatment. I must structure the UK deal so its terms are defensible as tailored to a principal supplying interest with an FTA, not a general template.

Not a party, but threatening tariff retaliation over the EU's Article XXVIII actions. Their pressure shortens my runway and raises the cost of a delayed or messy process — another reason to close with the UK quickly and cleanly.

parties.who: The Commissioner and my own chain in DG TRADE
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A deal done on time, within mandate, that preserves the regime's integrity and requires no embarrassing return to Council for a revised mandate. They want no surprises and no headlines about EU-UK trade conflict on top of the US dispute.

objectives: Secure a tariff rate quota volume and allocation method that preserves the large majority of current UK duty-free access: ideally a country-specific UK allocation at or near recent trade levels (~2.4Mt), rather than a 400kt global first-come first-served pool in which UK exporters compete against Turkey and Korea.
Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate well below 50%, or carve out the product lines where UK exports are concentrated (the narrower range where the UK is a principal supplier).

Prevent or narrow the disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel — this is a red line issue because it strips preferences the UK holds under the TCA and sets a damaging precedent.
Secure a review clause and defined duration so the regime is not permanent by default.

Protect the ongoing working relationship with my EU counterpart and the UK's standing in Geneva committees, and avoid being drawn into the Japan/Korea joint FTA dispute in a way that poisons the negotiation.
Reach a settlement London can clear by June rather than gambling on no-deal retaliation, given how exposed the UK steel industry is.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settled package London can accept that keeps most UK steel exports flowing duty-free (country-specific allocation at meaningful volume, a bearable out-of-quota rate, TCA treatment intact or largely intact, plus a review clause) before the June deadline, with the relationship and other goods files intact. Failure is either no settlement — leaving the UK with 400kt global FCFS access, a 50% out-of-quota rate and a slow, uncertain retaliation path — or a settlement so close to the EU's opening offer that London cannot clear it or the industry is destroyed anyway. Quietly losing the FTA-disapplication point while winning volume would be a partial, bitter success; losing both is failure.
declaration.approach: I will open by testing the EU's flexibility on architecture (country-specific allocation vs global FCFS) before haggling on volume, because allocation method determines the real value of any tonnage figure. I will make an early, real concession — signalling UK willingness to guarantee EU exporters' treatment under our own steel measure and Article XXVIII process — since momentum pays and this is the leverage the EU most wants, but I will bank it against a concrete EU move rather than give it free. I will remind the EU of their June Council timeline and that no-deal leaves them facing UK retaliation across 3.6Mt of EU steel exports plus parallel claims from Turkey, Korea, India and Japan. I will keep the Japan/Korea joint-dispute idea at arm's length: useful as background pressure London can hint at, but I will not let it derail the table. Throughout, I will report honestly to London on the gap between the EU's offer and our landing zone, and press for a settlement figure as soon as the EU's shape of a deal becomes visible.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, clean settlement before the June Council vote that locks in as much of the notified regime as possible; minimum compensation; UK commitments on treatment of EU steel under the UK's own measure; and no precedent that complicates their separate Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims.

Steel-producing member states will defend the 50% rate and small quota; steel-consuming member states and exporters will quietly want UK market access preserved under the UK measure; the Council wants this off the table on schedule with the 'non-market economy overcapacity' rationale intact.

A deal that saves the UK steel industry and can be sold domestically; they fear no-deal but also cannot clear a deal near the EU's opening offer; they will weigh using the UK's own steel measure and retaliation as leverage.

To recruit the UK into a joint FTA dispute over the disapplication of FTA provisions, adding pressure on the EU; they care about the precedent, not about UK quota volumes, and their interests diverge from mine if their tactics disrupt my settlement.

Their own compensation in parallel tracks; Turkey and Korea ship more than the UK, so a global FCFS quota advantages them — a UK country-specific allocation is partly at their expense, which the EU will use against me.

parties.who: UK steel industry and domestic stakeholders
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Survival: maximum duty-free access to the EU market, which takes 75% of UK exports; they will judge any deal harshly if volumes fall far below current trade.

objectives: Secure a tariff-free quota volume materially above 400,000 tonnes, ideally approaching a significant share of the UK's 2.4 million tonnes of annual exports to the EU, or at minimum sufficient to keep the two at-risk plants viable

Obtain a UK country-specific quota allocation rather than a global first-come-first-served pool, so UK exporters are not crowded out by larger suppliers (Turkey, Korea) racing to fill the quota early in each period
Remove or water down the proposed legal text disapplying FTA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel — preserving TCA preferences is a red-line objective
Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate well below 50% if quota volume concessions are insufficient
Secure a review clause and limited duration so this is not a permanent 50% bound ceiling
Protect UK steel-consuming manufacturers by limiting collateral damage from any UK retaliation and avoiding a spiral with the EU
Conclude within the four rounds so the UK avoids the default outcome (400kt global FCFS at 50%), which would likely kill the two plants
declaration.success_and_failure: Success means a signed outcome that gives UK producers reliable, predictable tariff-free access at a volume large enough that the two at-risk plants' owners judge continued investment worthwhile — which in practice means a country-specific UK allocation well above 400kt, preservation of TCA preferences, a review clause, and ideally a lower out-of-quota rate. A good deal could trade improved EU country-specific quota shares under the UK's own safeguard for these gains. Partial success is a deal that is commercially survivable for the industry even if imperfect, allowing ministers to pair it with the domestic subsidy package. Failure is either no settlement (leaving the default 400kt global FCFS regime, which likely triggers plant closures and forces UK retaliation six months later) or a settlement so weak that the plants close anyway and I am answerable for having given away leverage — such as UK safeguard allocations — for nothing. I will also judge myself on whether I preserved the UK-EU trading relationship enough to avoid wider damage to the 3.6mt of EU steel the UK imports.
declaration.approach: I will instruct the Geneva seat to move early and constructively — momentum pays. The UK's core leverage is threefold: (1) we hold principal supplying interest status and the EU cannot conclude without negotiating with us, though they can proceed without agreement; (2) we run a parallel Article XXVIII process on our own steel safeguard where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas worth 3.6mt of access — I have permission to offer improved EU country-specific allocations there in exchange for significant concessions; (3) failure costs the EU too, since we could withdraw substantially equivalent concessions within six months. My strategy is to open by linking the two files: offer meaningful improvements to EU quotas under the UK safeguard in return for a large UK-specific quota (target: at least 1.5–2mt equivalent), preservation of TCA tariff treatment, and a review clause. I will not reveal the domestic subsidy fallback — it is my insurance against signing a bad deal, not a substitute for a good one. I will push hard on allocation method, because a global FCFS quota at any volume disadvantages the UK's concentrated product mix against Turkey and Korea's larger volumes. If the EU resists on volume, I will trade down on the out-of-quota rate and product carve-outs for the specific lines the UK ships. I will keep the back-pocket threat of substantially equivalent retaliation credible but unstated early, deploying it in later rounds if the EU stalls. I will aim to have a package ministers can clear by Round 3, leaving Round 4 as a margin.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, clean conclusion before June so the Council can vote on schedule; to hold the 50% bound rate and keep the TRQ small and globally allocated to maximise protection for EU producers; to keep the FTA-disapplication text to target non-market economy circumvention; to avoid UK retaliation that would hit EU exporters in the UK safeguard; they may be flexible on allocation method and review clauses if we give them something on the UK safeguard file.

Steel-producing member states will want maximum protection and resist country-specific carve-outs; steel-consuming member states will want cheap imports and may quietly favour larger quotas. The June deadline pressures them toward a deal, but they will test whether the UK blinks first.

parties.who: UK steel industry and plant owners
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Guaranteed, predictable tariff-free access volumes sufficient to justify continued investment at the two at-risk sites; they will judge any deal on whether it keeps order books viable, not on legal niceties.
Continued access to EU steel imports at reasonable prices; they will oppose aggressive UK retaliation that raises their input costs.
A politically presentable win that keeps the plants open without committing the full subsidy package; they are heavily invested and will clear a deal that can be defended as saving the industry.

Not at this table, but their claims constrain the EU: any country-specific allocation given to the UK sets a precedent and shrinks the residual quota for larger suppliers. The EU will cite this to resist UK-specific shares; I should be ready to argue the UK's PSI status and concentrated product range justify distinct treatment.

public_message: Thank you. Brussels has asked me to open this process formally and constructively. The Article XXVIII modification will proceed; the question for us is whether we can put it on a stable, rules-consistent footing and avoid wider escalation. As an opening signal, I am authorised to move away from a purely global first-come-first-served model toward country-specific allocation with licensing, to increase the pool to 800,000 tonnes, and to identify a UK tranche of 400,000 tonnes within it, with an out-of-quota bound rate of 40%, eight-year duration and a review at year four. I can also scope the draft so that TCA preferences for UK-originating steel are preserved inside the agreed tranche rather than disapplied there, provided we have robust melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention discipline. In exchange I need the UK to keep this inside Article XXVIII, not join or encourage an FTA dispute track, indicate priority compensation lines, and give reciprocal stability for EU exporters under the UK steel measure.

other_terms: licensing based on recent historical trade, quarterly openings, limited carry-over
TCA preferential treatment preserved for UK-originating steel within the UK tranche
melt-and-pour origin evidence and anti-circumvention/transhipment controls
compensation to be valued across the EU schedule; UK to identify priority lines
reciprocal stability for EU exporters under the UK's steel measure and country-specific quotas

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A sharp counter anchored on historic UK flows, likely demanding a tranche closer to recent export volumes, rejection of any out-of-quota rate above low single digits, and full withdrawal of the FTA-disapplication text.
expectations.why: The UK has principal supplying interest and high exposure; it will test whether early EU movement implies more volume is available.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Instructions to probe compensation and TCA interaction while avoiding commitment to restraint on the Japan/Korea dispute idea until a clearer package emerges.
expectations.why: Domestic steel pressure makes the capital more demanding than the Geneva room, but it also needs a sellable outcome quickly.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Continued effort to pull the UK toward a joint FTA response if the EU text keeps FTA disapplication.
expectations.why: They want leverage from UK alignment; visible EU-UK movement reduces the attraction of that path.

private_rationale: I have no settlement figure, so I should not open at the likely landing zone. But momentum matters and the main systemic risk is UK drift into a Japan/Korea FTA dispute. I therefore give early movement on architecture, administration, duration/review and partial TCA scoping, while keeping volume and out-of-quota rate deliberately short. A 400k UK tranche inside an 800k pool is defensible as an opening because it is double the notified pool and changes the allocation principle, yet leaves room to move on tonnage, product carve-outs and compensation later. Linking to UK treatment of EU exporters creates reciprocity without formally merging the two Article XXVIII processes.

public_message: Thank you. I take the move on country-specific allocation, licensing, a larger pool and TCA treatment inside the tranche as a constructive signal, and I am prepared to build on it. But I have to be clear: a 400,000 tonne UK tranche against 2.4 million tonnes of recent trade is not a compensation basis; it is a managed contraction of the UK industry and London will not be able to present it as Article XXVIII balance. Our counter is a 4.0 million tonne pool with a 1.8 million tonne UK tranche, country-specific and licence-administered on a recent-reference basis, out-of-quota bound rate no higher than 25%, five-year duration with review at year three, and no blanket disapplication of TCA preferences for UK-originating steel. We can accept disciplined melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention provisions where they are proportionate and do not operate as a hidden quota cut. If the EU moves materially toward that scale, I can recommend that we keep this strictly inside Article XXVIII, discourage a parallel FTA dispute track, exchange priority compensation lines for any residual gap, and address reciprocal predictability for EU exporters under the UK measure as part of the same package rather than as a standalone concession.

other_terms: UK tranche set by recent-reference period with licensing, not first-come first-served
No blanket disapplication of TCA preferences for UK-originating steel; preferences preserved at least within the tranche and administration must not nullify them
Proportionate melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention rules with consultation before remedies and no retroactive duty shocks
Review at year three; extension beyond five years only by mutual agreement
Residual gap below recent UK trade to be offset by concessions on mutually identified EU schedule lines
Reciprocal stability for EU exporters under the UK steel measure only as part of an overall package
Targeted carve-outs for concentrated UK product lines where EU supply dependence is high

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A rejection of the headline numbers as outside mandate, but movement above 800,000 total pool and 400,000 UK tranche, with probing on compensation lines and the UK measure.
expectations.why: The EU has signalled flexibility early and faces the June Council vote, but needs to show it extracted UK discipline on disputes and reciprocity.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Instruction to hold a high anchor, keep the dispute track warm but not activated, and seek clarity on how far the EU can move before the Council timetable bites.
expectations.why: No settlement figure has been given and the EU opening is described as industry-destroying, so capital will want leverage preserved.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Continued pressure to join or encourage an FTA dispute and disapply FTA benefits in retaliation.
expectations.why: They gain leverage if the UK hardens, but early escalation would narrow the Article XXVIII space the UK currently needs.

private_rationale: I am anchoring high because 400,000 tonnes is only one-sixth of recent UK exports and accepting anything near it would foreclose London's options. A 4.0 million pool with 1.8 million for the UK is still below recent trade, so it is defensible as compensation plus partial adjustment rather than full replication, while leaving room to concede later. I trade process reassurance now — staying in Article XXVIII, resisting Japan/Korea escalation, offering compensation-line exchange and conditional reciprocity — because early movement should draw EU movement, but I do not concede the UK measure unconditionally or accept the FTA-disapplication text.

report: I opened with a material move away from the notified position: an 800,000-tonne pool, a 400,000-tonne UK country-specific tranche, licensing, a 40% out-of-quota bound rate, eight-year duration, review at year four, and preservation of TCA preferences within the UK tranche subject to melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention discipline. I linked this to the UK remaining within Article XXVIII, not joining an FTA dispute, identifying compensation priorities and providing stability for EU exporters under the UK measure. The UK welcomed the direction but rejected the scale as incapable of compensating its 2.4 million tonnes of recent trade. It countered with a 4.0 million-tonne pool, a 1.8 million-tonne UK tranche, country-specific licensing on a recent-reference basis, an out-of-quota rate no higher than 25%, five-year duration and review at year three. It also seeks an end to blanket TCA disapplication. In return, it indicated willingness to keep the matter in Article XXVIII, discourage a joint FTA dispute, discuss compensation lines for any residual gap and address reciprocal predictability for EU exporters as part of the package.

recommendation.reasoning: The UK has given a clear de-escalation signal but requires material movement on volume and TCA treatment before it can move away from its maximalist counter. A controlled second move to a 1.2 million-tonne pool and 700,000-tonne UK tranche would preserve negotiating space while testing whether the UK will reduce its 1.8 million-tonne demand. Country-specific licensing, review at year three and preservation of TCA preferences within the tranche should be conditional on effective melt-and-pour enforcement, no UK participation in or encouragement of an FTA dispute, identification of compensation lines and reciprocal predictability for EU exporters under the UK measure. The out-of-quota rate should remain well above the UK demand of 25% at this stage.

requests.why: This is material enough to test the UK's stated willingness to de-escalate while leaving room before any eventual landing zone.

requests.why: A modest rate movement reinforces momentum without conceding the UK's opening demand.

requests.why: This narrows the duration gap and may be less costly than additional volume.

instruction: Make a controlled second move, but do not lead with the full authority. Open Round 2 at a 1,000,000-tonne pool with a 550,000-tonne UK country-specific tranche, licence-administered on a recent-reference basis. You may move up to 1,200,000 tonnes overall and 700,000 tonnes for the UK only if the UK moves materially from its 1.8 million-tonne demand and accepts the package conditions. report: The EU opened materially above its notified position: an 800,000-tonne pool, a 400,000-tonne UK country-specific tranche, licensing, a 40% out-of-quota bound rate, eight-year duration, review at year four, and preservation of TCA preferences within the UK tranche subject to melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention discipline. In return, it asked the UK to keep the matter within Article XXVIII, stay out of a parallel FTA dispute, identify priority compensation lines, and provide reciprocal stability for EU exporters under the UK steel measure. I welcomed the procedural movement but made clear that 400,000 tonnes against 2.4 million tonnes of recent UK trade could not be presented as Article XXVIII balance. I tabled a 4.0 million-tonne pool, a 1.8 million-tonne UK tranche, country-specific licensing on a recent-reference basis, a maximum 25% out-of-quota rate, five-year duration with review at year three, and no blanket disapplication of TCA preferences. I indicated that proportionate anti-circumvention rules, priority compensation lines and reciprocal predictability for EU exporters could form part of a package if the EU moved materially on scale. No agreement is close yet, but the EU has shown that its allocation model, pool size and TCA treatment are negotiable.

We should maintain our ambitious counter, require a substantial EU move on the UK tranche and out-of-quota rate in Round 2, and only then sequence movement on compensation lines, dispute-track restraint and reciprocal treatment for EU exporters.

instruction: Good work in Round 1. The EU's opening confirms they are under time pressure and that allocation model, pool size and TCA treatment are all movable. Do not settle anything near 400,000 tonnes. In Round 2, hold the shape of our counter but show controlled momentum on the elements that cost us least: you may signal flexibility on total pool size (down from 4.0m toward 3.0m) and on duration/review timing, but hold firm on the UK tranche at or near 1.8m and the 25% out-of-quota rate for now. Make clear that the UK tranche is the core of Article XXVIII balance given 2.4m tonnes of recent trade, and that any EU movement on the tranche unlocks movement from us on (a) compensation lines, (b) predictability for EU exporters under our safeguard, and (c) dispute-track restraint. You may state that the UK intends to keep this within Article XXVIII while substantive progress continues — conditional language only, no waiver of FTA or WTO rights. You may discuss melt-and-pour and licensing technically, but only on the basis that these are verification disciplines, not volume restrictions. Do not table any fallback on the tranche in Round 2. Do not agree or close anything; all conclusions require my clearance and ministerial sign-off. Probe what sits behind their 800,000 pool figure — if Turkey and Korea hold larger claims, the UK tranche share of any pool matters as much as the headline number.

authority.notes: These are outer bounds for any eventual agreement, not for tabling. Geneva may not agree to a UK tranche below 1,200,000 tonnes, an out-of-quota rate above 30%, a total pool below 2,000,000 tonnes, or any arrangement without country-specific licensed allocation and a review clause. Duration 5 years preferred; may stretch to 7 with a review at year 3. TCA preferences for UK-originating steel must be preserved across the full tranche, not merely 'scoped' — no blanket disapplication is acceptable at any tranche size. Melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention provisions acceptable only if: based on standard certification and existing customs data, licensing is automatic or near-automatic, no additional testing or registration burden that operates as a de facto volume cut, and quota-fill is monitored with unused tranche capacity reallocated. Any offer of improved EU allocations under the UK safeguard requires my explicit sign-off first — flag before offering.

Anything outside these bounds comes back to me and ministers before agreement.

response_to_requests.why: Granted, but sequenced. You may discuss compensation lines only in general, indicative terms in Round 2 and only after the EU has moved materially on the UK tranche. No specific lines named until Round 3 at the earliest, and nothing binding at any point without my clearance. Compensation is our trade coin for closing any residual gap between the EU's best tranche offer and our 1.2m floor — do not spend it early.

response_to_requests.request: Guidance on the maximum reciprocal predictability the UK can offer EU exporters under the UK steel measure, including whether country-specific EU allocations can be discussed and what safeguards are required.
response_to_requests.why: Not yet. Ministers have authorised improved EU country-specific quota allocations under our safeguard, but only in exchange for significant EU concessions, and this must be co-ordinated with our own Article XXVIII process. In Round 2 you may acknowledge this as discussable 'in a final package' but offer nothing specific. If the EU moves the tranche toward 1.2m in Round 3, come back to me and I will authorise a defined uplift. Premature specificity here spends our best coin and risks undercutting our own safeguard negotiation.

response_to_requests.why: Granted on exactly those terms: process restraint is conditional on continued substantive progress, is expressed as current intent, and expressly reserves all rights under the TCA and WTO agreements. This is cheap reassurance that buys goodwill and keeps pressure from other members' interest in parallel tracks as latent leverage.

response_to_requests.why: Granted as set out in the authority notes: standard certification and customs data only, automatic or near-automatic licensing, no testing or registration burdens that reduce usable quota, transparent quota-fill monitoring, and reallocation of unused tranche capacity. Test every EU enforcement proposal against one question: does this reduce the tonnes the UK industry can actually ship? If yes, it counts against the tranche number and we say so explicitly at the table.

private_rationale: The EU's opening move off its notified position in Round 1 confirms they need a deal before June as much as we do — their Council timetable is fixed and the notified fallback (400,000-tonne global FCFS quota) is worse for us but also messy for them with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan holding rights. My strategy: land this in Round 3 or early Round 4 at a UK tranche of 1.2–1.5m tonnes, out-of-quota rate of 25–30%, country-specific licensing, TCA preferences preserved in full, 5–6 year duration with review. The tranche floor of 1.2m is calibrated to what keeps the two at-risk plants viable when combined with the subsidisation package ministers are considering — I have not told Geneva this, because a negotiator who knows the floor will drift toward it. If the EU's best final tranche lands between 1.0m and 1.2m, I can still construct a presentable package using compensation lines plus the subsidy announcement, but that requires ministerial sign-off and I will not pre-authorise it. The EU safeguard allocation uplift is held back deliberately: it is the one concession that costs our domestic industry something, so it must be the last thing tabled, exchanged for the single biggest EU move. Round 2 is about holding position, conceding only on pool headline and duration, and extracting their second move.

reasoning: Round 1 opened a genuine negotiation but no agreed terms exist: the UK countered at a 4.0M-tonne pool, 1.8M-tonne UK tranche and 25% out-of-quota rate against our 800,000/400,000/40% opening. Accepting anything now would lock in terms far outside both my mandate ceilings and the UK's position. The UK has signalled de-escalation conditional on material movement, which Round 2's authorised controlled move (1.0M pool, 550,000 UK tranche, stepping toward 1.2M/700,000, 35%, six years with year-three review) is designed to test. With four rounds available, US retaliation pressure on us, and the UK's no-deal exposure being worse than ours, there is no case for either accepting the default or closing now. Continue and trade movement strictly against UK movement on volume plus the non-dispute, origin-enforcement and UK-measure conditions.

The EU's opening offer (800,000-tonne pool, 400,000-tonne UK tranche, 40% out-of-quota rate) is far outside the authorised settlement bounds — minimum 1.2m UK tranche, minimum 2m pool, maximum 30% out-of-quota rate — and would be indefensible to ministers and the industry against 2.4m tonnes of recent trade. Accepting now would lock in a severe managed contraction of the UK steel sector, and I have no authority to agree anything near these terms. Equally, letting the process lapse (accept_default) would leave the notified 400,000-tonne global first-come-first-served quota with no review clause as the outcome — the worst case for the UK. The EU's first-round movement on allocation model, pool size, licensing and TCA treatment confirms genuine negotiating space and time pressure on their side. The right course is to continue, hold the UK tranche and out-of-quota rate firm in Round 2, show controlled flexibility on pool size and duration, and sequence our movement on compensation lines, EU safeguard predictability and dispute-track restraint strictly against EU movement on the tranche.

public_message: Thank you. I take your counter in the constructive spirit in which I hope my opening was received, and Brussels has authorised me to move again. I can now put on the table a total pool of 1,000,000 tonnes, with a UK country-specific tranche of 550,000 tonnes, licence-administered on a recent-reference basis. On duration, I can offer six years with a review at year three — though I must be clear the review would examine operation and market conditions; it could not automatically alter agreed volumes, allocation or rates. I confirm that TCA preferences for UK-originating steel would be preserved inside the UK tranche, subject to melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention discipline, with all preferential access counting within that tranche rather than any separate FTA pool. On the out-of-quota rate, I hold at 40% for now; 25% is not within any landing zone I can presently describe to Brussels. Two further points. First, scale: your 1.8 million tonne tranche and 4.0 million tonne pool remain far beyond anything my capital could conclude. I have moved substantially toward you on structure and volume; I need to see material movement from your side before I can return to Brussels again — and I will be candid that I have some room to do so if that movement comes. Second, the package conditions: I need an explicit UK commitment not to initiate, join, encourage or coordinate any FTA or WTO dispute concerning this measure — I accept you cannot bind third parties, but your own position matters. I also invite you to identify concrete priority compensation lines, and I am looking for reciprocal predictability for EU exporters under the UK steel measure: no worsening of EU country-specific access for at least three years, transparent administration, and advance consultation before changes. On the FTA disapplication outside the tranche, I cannot concede its removal; at most I can agree that its operation would be examined at the year-three review.

public_message: Thank you. I welcome the further movement: a larger pool, a larger UK tranche, recent-reference licensing, six years with review at year three, and confirmation that TCA preferences for UK-originating steel are preserved inside the tranche. That is real movement and I will report it as such. But I must be equally clear: 550,000 tonnes remains far from any balance we can defend against 2.4 million tonnes of recent trade, and a 40% out-of-quota rate with FTA disapplication maintained outside the tranche compounds that rather than compensates for it. My capital has authorised me to show momentum where we can. On the total pool, I move from 4.0 to 3.0 million tonnes. On duration, I can accept six years with review at year three, though the review must be capable of adjusting volumes and rates in light of market conditions, not merely examining operation — a review that cannot bite is not a review clause we can present as balance. The UK tranche at 1.8 million tonnes and a 25% out-of-quota bound rate remain the core of Article XXVIII equivalence on our side, and I am not in a position to move on either today. On your three conditions: the UK intends to keep this within Article XXVIII while substantive progress continues — that is a statement of current intent, not a waiver of rights, and its durability depends on the landing zone. On compensation lines, I am ready to begin technical discussion of an indicative hierarchy once I see the EU's next move on the tranche. On reciprocal predictability under our steel measure, I understand the ask — no worsening of EU country-specific access for a period, transparent administration, advance consultation — but any offer there requires explicit clearance from my capital, and I will flag it for them alongside your movement today; expect a substantive answer next round. On enforcement, we can accept melt-and-pour and anti-circumvention disciplines based on standard certification and existing customs data, with automatic or near-automatic licensing, monitored quota-fill and reallocation of unused tranche capacity — verification, not a disguised volume cut. Finally, one question that matters to the arithmetic: what do you envisage the balance of the pool to be against Turkey and Korea's claims? The UK tranche's share of the pool matters as much as the headline number, and I will need to understand the composition before London can assess any further movement from us.

private_rationale: London instructed me to hold the 1.8m tranche and 25% rate, move the pool from 4.0m toward 3.0m, show flexibility on duration/review, and table no tranche fallback in Round 2. I pushed the review to be substantive rather than cosmetic because London's outer bounds require a review clause with teeth, and I probed pool composition because a 550k UK tranche inside a 1.0m pool against Turkish and Korean claims may signal the EU's internal ceiling is lower than stated — the answer will tell London whether their real landing zone on the tranche is near 1.2m or well below. I converted the dispute ask into conditional intent language as authorised, deferred compensation lines to keep them as trade coin, and punted the safeguard ask to London as required, while committing to answer next round to keep the EU engaged. report: Round 2 closed with movement on both sides but a large gap remaining. I opened at 1.0M tonnes pool / 550,000-tonne UK tranche (holding back the 1.2M/700k ceilings), six years with review at year three limited to examining operation, TCA preferences preserved inside the UK tranche with all preferential access counting against it, 40% out-of-quota rate held, and my three package conditions (non-dispute commitment, compensation priorities, UK-measure predictability). The UK responded with real but limited movement: pool demand cut from 4.0M to 3.0M, acceptance of six-year duration, but review must be capable of adjusting volumes and rates — not merely examining them. It held firm at 1.8M UK tranche and 25% out-of-quota rate, stating it cannot move on either today. On my conditions: non-dispute was framed as 'current intent while substantive progress continues', explicitly not a waiver and contingent on the landing zone; compensation-line hierarchy offered only after our next move on the tranche; UK-measure predictability (no worsening of EU access, transparency, advance consultation) has been flagged to London with a substantive answer promised next round. On enforcement it offered standard certification, automatic licensing, monitored quota-fill and reallocation of unused capacity — verification, not a disguised cut, which is broadly workable. Critically, it asked what balance of the pool we envisage against Turkey and Korea's claims, signalling its share of the pool matters as much as the headline. It has not yet moved off 1.8M, so I have not deployed the 700k ceiling.

recommendation.reasoning: The UK has moved on pool (4.0M to 3.0M) and duration and has promised substantive answers next round on the UK measure and a compensation hierarchy — momentum is real and the dispute-track risk is currently contained by 'intent'. But it has explicitly held the two core parameters (1.8M tranche, 25% rate) and demanded a review with teeth. Deploying our ceilings now would spend our remaining room against an unmoved UK position. The UK's question on Turkey/Korea pool composition is the opening: if we can present a coherent composition in which the UK share is defensible, and London delivers on the UK-measure answer and compensation hierarchy, that is the moment to move toward the ceiling. Round 3 should test whether the UK's 'not today' on the tranche is a sequencing position or a floor.

instruction: Good handling of Round 2. The UK has moved on pool and duration, promised substantive answers on its steel measure and a compensation hierarchy, and asked the composition question — that question is your lever for Round 3, use it deliberately. You may deploy the ceiling, but staged, as you proposed. Open Round 3 by presenting indicative pool composition: describe the UK tranche at the ceiling level (700,000 within 1,200,000, roughly 58% of the pool) as reflecting the UK's concentrated product range and principal supplying interest, and make clear the UK tranche is a locked, country-specific allocation whose value cannot be eroded by whatever we agree with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan in their separate processes — their claims are handled separately and do not dilute the UK tranche. Presenting the 58% share is your way of moving toward the ceiling; if the UK responds with material movement off 1.8 million tonnes, you may put 1.1 million / 620,000 formally on the table, and reserve the full 1.2 million / 700,000 for demonstrated movement plus delivery on the package conditions. I am extending a final-reserve margin: if, and only if, the UK moves below roughly 1.3 million tonnes on its tranche demand AND delivers both the firm non-dispute commitment and a substantive UK-measure offer, you may go to 750,000 tonnes for the UK within the 1.2 million pool. That 750,000 is the absolute ceiling and must not be tabled before Round 4 unless the UK has already moved below 1.3 million. Hold the out-of-quota rate at 40% until the UK moves off 25%, then 35% is the floor — do not go below it. 25% remains outside any landing zone. On the review clause, you have new flexibility: you may accept that the year-three review can recommend adjustments to volumes or rates, but only where objective, pre-defined triggers are met (import surge relative to domestic demand, capacity utilisation below an agreed threshold), with any adjustment subject to mutual agreement, capped at plus or minus 15% of the agreed tranche volume, and exercisable once. No automatic alteration, no open-ended adjustment power — I will answer for this regime's operation and I cannot hand a future review a blank cheque. Hold the FTA disapplication outside the tranche; its operation may be examined at the review, nothing more, and all UK TCA-preferential access continues to count within the UK tranche. On the non-dispute commitment: 'current intent' is not sufficient for the full ceiling. For anything above 620,000 I need an explicit UK commitment not to initiate, join, encourage or coordinate an FTA or WTO dispute on this measure for the duration of the regime, acknowledging they cannot bind third parties. On the UK steel measure: press for the promised substantive answer before you deploy anything above 620,000 — no worsening of EU country-specific access for at least three years, transparent administration, advance consultation. Do not exchange tonnage for vague assurances. If the UK tables its compensation hierarchy, you may engage at technical level and indicate we are prepared to look seriously at industrial goods lines of UK export interest — reference machinery, chemicals and processed food categories as areas we could examine — but commit to nothing and value nothing in the room; any line requires member state consultation through the Trade Policy Committee. Remember the arithmetic of our position: no-deal hurts the UK far more than us, but we need agreement this month for the June Council vote. Do not say that to them. Land the negotiation in Round 3 if the UK moves; keep enough in reserve for Round 4 if it does not.

report: Round 2 saw further real EU movement. They raised the pool from 800,000 to 1,000,000 tonnes and the UK tranche from 400,000 to 550,000 tonnes, licence-administered on a recent-reference basis. They moved on duration to six years with review at year three, but qualified that the review could only examine operation and market conditions, not alter agreed volumes, allocation or rates. They confirmed TCA preferences for UK-originating steel preserved inside the UK tranche, with all preferential access counting within the tranche — i.e., no separate FTA pool on top. They held the out-of-quota rate at 40% and stated 25% is not currently describable to Brussels as a landing zone. They signalled clearly they have further room on tranche scale if we show material movement first. Their three conditions hardened: (a) an explicit UK commitment not to initiate, join, encourage or coordinate any FTA or WTO dispute on this measure (they accept we cannot bind third parties); (b) concrete priority compensation lines; (c) reciprocal predictability under our steel measure — no worsening of EU country-specific access for at least three years, transparent administration, advance consultation. On FTA disapplication outside the tranche, they will not remove it; at most they will agree its operation is examined at the year-three review. Per instructions, I moved only on pool (4.0m to 3.0m) and duration (accepted six years, but insisted the review must be capable of adjusting volumes and rates). I held the 1.8m tranche and 25% rate, gave conditional Article XXVIII restraint language, deferred compensation lines until their next tranche move, flagged the safeguard ask for your clearance with a substantive answer promised next round, set our technical parameters on melt-and-pour/licensing, and probed the pool composition against Turkey and Korea's claims. The gap on the core: we are at 1.8m/25%, they are at 550k/40%. They have conceded structure almost entirely (country-specific, licensed, recent-reference, TCA inside tranche); the fight from here is purely scale and rate, plus the review's teeth and the FTA disapplication tail.

instruction: Strong round. Their two moves confirm the momentum strategy is working and they are negotiating against their June deadline, not ours. For Round 3: you now have answers on all six of your requests — see below. The shape of the round: (1) Open by pressing the unanswered pool-composition question — make clear that London cannot assess any pool figure without knowing what Turkey and Korea's claims absorb, and that a 1.0m pool with two larger claimants than us is arithmetically inconsistent with a meaningful UK tranche; this supports our case that the pool must rise. (2) Answer their safeguard ask substantively, as promised: the UK is prepared to offer no worsening of EU country-specific access under our steel measure for three years, transparent administration, and advance consultation before changes — but table this only after, and explicitly in exchange for, their next tranche move; do not offer it speculatively. Do not offer improved EU allocations beyond a standstill — that requires my explicit sign-off and ministerial clearance. (3) If they move the tranche to 900k or above, you may move from 1.8m to 1.6m, paired with the safeguard standstill as a package. If they reach 1.1m or above, you may move to 1.4m. Do not go below 1.4m in Round 3 regardless of what they offer; 1.2m is an absolute floor and is never to be tabled. (4) Hold the out-of-quota rate at 25% throughout Round 3 — no movement on rate this round; rate movement is reserved for the endgame and is conditional on tranche and review teeth. (5) Table an indicative, explicitly non-binding compensation hierarchy: certain aluminium lines, certain chemical and fertiliser lines, certain agri-food lines, and certain machinery lines — framed as illustrative categories for technical-level development, conditional on the final tranche and rate, and not a commitment to any specific line. (6) On dispute restraint, reject their formulation. 'Not initiate, join, encourage or coordinate' is unacceptably broad — it would have us policing third parties and private actors and would surrender leverage we share with Japan and Korea. Counter-offer: the UK will not initiate or join a dispute concerning this measure while it operates as agreed, as part of the final package and contingent on mutual performance. (7) Make the review's teeth a formal, non-negotiable ask: the year-three review must be capable of adjusting volumes, allocation and rates in light of market conditions. A review that can only examine is a nullity and London cannot present it as balance. This is cheap for them to give — press it hard. (8) On FTA disapplication outside the tranche, continue to register that maintaining it compounds the access cut; at minimum it must fall within the scope of the year-three review with a presumption of remedy, not merely an examination of its operation. Do not close anything. Two rounds remain; we are converging, and I want them to feel that settling with us in Round 3 or 4 is achievable — but only on terms we can defend to ministers and industry.

Per your instructions I delivered the three gated items: the safeguard standstill (no worsening of EU country-specific access for three years, transparency, advance consultation — tabled explicitly in exchange for their tranche movement), the indicative non-binding compensation hierarchy (aluminium, chemicals/fertilisers, agri-food, machinery), and the scoped dispute-restraint formulation (UK will not initiate or join a dispute while the measure operates as agreed, contingent on mutual performance — rejecting 'encourage or coordinate'). I accepted the review architecture in principle subject to technical work on triggers and discussion of the 15% cap and single-use limit. I held 1.8m and 25% (their 620k–700k did not reach the 900k trigger for movement). I signalled — and flag this to you — that with the tranche lock in legal text, the headline pool is secondary to the tranche level, and that pool flexibility exists on our side if the tranche is right; I note this sits in tension with the 2.0m pool outer bound and I would welcome confirmation. I re-registered the FTA disapplication point (must sit within the year-three review with a presumption of remedy). One round remains. The structural elements are now all agreed or near-agreed: locked country-specific licensed tranche, recent-reference basis, TCA preferences preserved inside the tranche, a review with real teeth, safeguard standstill, compensation hierarchy, scoped restraint. The open fight is purely scale (700k visible EU ceiling vs our 1.8m ask / 1.2m floor) and the out-of-quota rate (40% vs 25%), plus the review cap and FTA disapplication tail.

recommendation.reasoning: Everything except scale and rate is now settled or settleable, which is a major achievement and worth protecting — but the core gap is stark: the EU has shown its ceiling (~700k) and it sits 500k below our absolute floor of 1.2m. Accepting anything near 700k/40% is not presentable to ministers or industry and breaches my authority; walking away now, with one round left and all structure agreed, forfeits the best-negotiated package available and hands us the notified default (400k global FCFS, 50%, no review), which is worse than any EU offer on the table. The only rational course is to use Round 4 to force a genuine endgame: a final, packaged UK move — tranche descent paired with a first move off 25% — conditioned explicitly on the EU breaking decisively above 700k, with the review cap, FTA disapplication remedy and compensation depth used as additional extractable value. The EU's June deadline means they must conclude in Round 4; that is our remaining leverage. But I must be candid: if 700k truly is their ceiling, no settlement within my current authority is possible, and London should decide now whether the floor moves, whether compensation can substitute for volume, or whether we prepare for the post-no-deal withdrawal of concessions.

instruction: Final round. Here is your endgame instruction; read it as a single integrated package, not a menu. (1) THE TRANCHE FLOOR MOVES. Ministers have judged that a defended settlement with maximum compensating value beats no-deal, given the notified default (400k global FCFS, 50%, no review) is worse than anything now on the table and the structure you have won (locked country-specific licensed tranche, recent-reference, TCA preserved inside the tranche, a review with teeth) is genuinely valuable and would be lost. New absolute floor: 850,000 tonnes. Never table it. Descent path, each step conditional on the EU's stated tranche figure in the room: EU at or above 750k unlocks our move to 1.15m; EU at or above 850k unlocks 1.0m; EU at or above 950k unlocks 900k. If they open Round 4 still at 700k, hold at 1.8m briefly, put the full package on the table as the basis for convergence, and force them to move first — their June deadline means this is their last round too. (2) RATE. You may make our first move off 25%, but only inside the package: move to 28% only if their tranche is at or above 850k AND the FTA disapplication outside the tranche is brought within the year-three review with a presumption of remedy; 30% is the absolute ceiling, reserved for a final closing move if the tranche reaches 950k or above. Do not concede 30% for anything less. (3) POOL. Confirmed: your signal stands. With the UK tranche legally locked against dilution by the Turkey/Korea/India/Japan processes, concede the pool toward their 1.2m figure explicitly in exchange for tranche tonnage — this is now authorised and supersedes the 2.0m outer bound. (4) SAFEGUARD. You are now authorised to offer, beyond the three-year standstill already tabled, modestly improved EU country-specific allocations under our steel safeguard — but only as the final coin, only if the tranche reaches 900k or above, and frame it as subject to UK ministerial clearance in the concluding exchange. Do not quantify improvements; agree the principle and the conditionality. (5) COMPENSATION. Invite them to quantify concrete line-level concessions within the hierarchy (aluminium, chemicals/fertilisers, agri-food, machinery), with priority to industrial goods lines of UK export interest. Make clear London will assess the package as Article XXVIII balance measured in value: the deeper the tranche shortfall against recent trade, the deeper the compensation schedule must be. This is genuinely substitutable, not merely supplementary — but it supplements the tranche, it does not replace the 850k floor. (6) REVIEW. Accept the trigger architecture. Push the cap from 15% to 20% and single use to two uses; if forced to choose, prioritise the 20% cap. Trigger definitions: surge measured relative to the three-year reference average, capacity utilisation threshold set so that current depressed conditions can qualify — the review must be capable of moving volumes up in today's market, not only down. FTA disapplication must sit inside the review with a presumption of remedy. (7) DISPUTE RESTRAINT. Hold the narrow formulation exactly as tabled — no 'encourage or coordinate' under any circumstances. (8) CLOSING. Do not conclude in the room; report the best final EU package and I will seek ministerial clearance within the round. If their genuine, final ceiling is below 850k, do not settle — close the round cleanly, preserve the record of their structural concessions, and we move to the fallback.

private_rationale: The EU has shown 700k and said it is their horizon; our standing floor was 1.2m, so without a floor move Round 4 was guaranteed to fail. Moving the floor to 850k is defensible: it is more than double the notified default quota, country-specific and legally locked rather than global FCFS, with TCA preferences preserved inside it, a review that can add ~15-20% on objective triggers, rate relief to 28-30% from 50%, a deep compensation schedule, and the subsidy programme as domestic cover for the residual industry pain. The improved EU safeguard allocations are held back as the very last coin at >=900k because that is the only concession we have that the EU demonstrably wants and cannot get elsewhere, and it must buy tonnage, not goodwill. The descent triggers are spaced so every UK step requires a larger EU step, keeping the exchange ratio in our favour. If 700k is genuinely immovable, we walk: the notified default is bad, but settling at ~700k would be politically indistinguishable from capitulation and would weaken our position in the parallel Turkey/Korea processes and any subsequent retaliation design. The six-month retaliation window and the Japan/Korea track are our post-failure leverage and must be prepared, not improvised.

reasoning: No common terms are yet on the table: the UK is still formally at a 1.8 million tonne tranche and 25% out-of-quota rate, while the EU has tabled only 620,000 tonnes within 1.1 million and held 40%. Accepting now is impossible and accepting the default would sacrifice the June Council timeline and the substantial UK movement already obtained. The UK has delivered real value in Round 3: a three-year steel-measure standstill with transparency and advance consultation, an indicative compensation hierarchy, acceptance of the locked-tranche concept, acceptance in principle of the trigger-based review, and a scoped commitment not to initiate or join a dispute while the measure operates as agreed. The correct course is to use the final round to table the authorised integrated package: 750,000 tonnes locked within a reduced 1.1 million pool, rising to 800,000 only on same-round UK acceptance of 35%, the scoped restraint commitment and confirmation of the steel-measure standstill.

The EU's latest formal offer remains unacceptable: 620,000 tonnes, or potentially 700,000 tonnes conditionally, is below the 850,000-tonne absolute floor, and the 40% out-of-quota rate exceeds the authorised ceiling. The structural progress is nevertheless substantial, including a legally protected country-specific tranche, licensing, preserved TCA preferences within the tranche and a potentially meaningful review. With one round remaining and the notified default clearly worse, the UK should continue and use the final round to test whether the EU can reach an acceptable tranche and rate package.

public_message:
Thank you. You gave us three substantive deliverables last round, and I told Brussels so — the steel-measure standstill, the compensation hierarchy, and the scoped restraint commitment were reported as real movement and they have shaped what I can table today. This is the final round of this process, so let me be direct: what follows is the EU's final package. It is integrated, and it stands or falls as a whole.

First, scale and structure, responding directly to your signal that flexibility on the pool exists if the tranche is right. We restructure: a locked UK tranche of 750,000 tonnes within a reduced total pool of 1,100,000 tonnes — a UK share of roughly 68%, licence-administered on a recent-reference basis, protected in legal text from dilution or reallocation by our separate processes with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan. That is movement on both scale and share simultaneously, and it is more than double the notified global quota from which this process began.

Second, the out-of-quota rate: 35%. That is the floor of what Brussels can conclude, and I cannot move below it. Third, the review clause, where I can move: the year-three review can recommend adjustments on the objective triggers we discussed, subject to mutual agreement and single exercise — and I can move the cap from 15% to 20%, with a review of the cap itself at year five, specifically in exchange for your acceptance of 35% rather than 25%. Fourth, the FTA disapplication: I can agree that its operation falls within the year-three trigger-based review with a presumption that demonstrated injury to UK-originating trade will be remedied — but remedies flow through the same trigger, mutual-agreement and cap architecture, and the disapplication remains in force outside the tranche until then. I cannot concede removal. All UK TCA-preferential access continues to count within the tranche, and TCA preferences for UK-originating steel are preserved inside it.

Fifth, the package conditions, restated so there is no ambiguity: your restraint commitment in the form you offered — the UK will not initiate or join a dispute concerning this measure while it operates as agreed, contingent on mutual performance — is acceptable to Brussels as drafted. We no longer ask for 'encourage or coordinate'. And the steel-measure standstill as tabled: no worsening of EU country-specific access for three years, transparent administration, advance consultation.

Finally, one further element, and I am being fully transparent about how it works. If, in this round, you accept the 35% rate, confirm the restraint commitment and the steel-measure standstill, and accept this package, I am authorised to take the UK tranche to 800,000 tonnes, with the pool held at 1,000,000 tonnes — a UK share of 80%, locked. That figure exists to close this negotiation; it is not available incrementally and it does not survive this round.

On compensation, we will engage seriously and at technical level on your hierarchy — aluminium, chemicals and fertilisers, agri-food, machinery — subject, as you understand, to Trade Policy Committee consultation, with no line commitments or valuations in the room today.

Let me be equally clear about the alternative, because it matters for how both capitals read this. If this package is not accepted, the EU proceeds as notified: a 400,000-tonne quota, global, first-come first-served, no country-specific allocation, no locked tranche, no TCA preservation inside any tranche, no review clause — and no standstill or restraint commitments, because there would be no package to attach them to. Against that baseline, what is on the table today is a locked UK allocation of up to 800,000 tonnes — an 80% share — with preferential treatment preserved, a review that can bite, and predictability for exporters on both sides. That is the choice I am asking London to put to ministers.

public_message: Thank you. You have been direct with me, and this is the final round, so I will be direct with you. First, the record, because it matters. Across four rounds the EU has moved from a 400,000-tonne global first-come-first-served quota at 50% with no review to a locked, country-specific, licence-administered UK tranche on a recent-reference basis, protected in legal text from dilution by your parallel processes with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan; TCA preferences for UK-originating steel preserved inside the tranche; a year-three review with objective triggers that can move volumes, now with a 20% cap; the FTA disapplication brought within that review with a presumption of remedy for demonstrated injury; and acceptance of our restraint formulation exactly as drafted. Those are real, structural concessions and I will report them to London as such. I also acknowledge the pool restructure and the share you describe — you responded to our signal and I note it. The 50,000-tonne gap and 5-point rate difference are materially smaller than the value of what a no-deal destroys — the locked 80% share, TCA preservation inside the tranche, a review with teeth capable of lifting the tranche toward 960,000, our restraint formulation accepted, and the standstill. Against the notified default of 400,000 tonnes global first-come-first-served at 50% with no lock, no TCA preservation and no review, this package doubles the secured volume and preserves the legal architecture. Ministers judge this defensible to Parliament and the industry, with the compensation schedule and domestic support measures addressing the residual gap.

private_rationale: I recommended the 850k/30% bounds before the final package shape was visible, and Geneva was right to force the decision up to ministerial level rather than improvise. The honest arithmetic: 800k versus 850k is 50,000 tonnes — roughly 2% of recent trade — and 35% versus 30% bites only on out-of-quota volumes that will be thin in any case. Against that, a no-deal costs the entire structure: no lock, no 80% share, no TCA preservation, no review, no standstill, and a 400k global FCFS quota in which Turkey and Korea out-ship us and in which our guaranteed allocation is zero. Retaliation within six months punishes EU exporters but restores not one tonne of UK steel access, and the industry — with two plants on the brink — needs presentable certainty now, not leverage in eighteen months. The review clause is the sleeper value: triggers defined so current depressed conditions qualify means a realistic path to 960k at year three, above the floor I originally set, without further negotiation. The compensation schedule on industrial goods plus the subsidisation package ministers hold in reserve covers the residual political exposure. Ministers accept that presenting 'double the notified quota, locked, with preferences preserved and a review that can only be triggered upward in today's market' alongside domestic support is survivable in a way that 'we walked away over 50,000 tonnes and got the 400k global default' is not. The risk accepted: the EU Council could still degrade the legal text in June — hence keeping the retaliation design warm and making clear our restraint is contingent on mutual performance.

reasoning: This is the EU's own final package at its closing configuration, tabled in Round 4 and confirmed within mandate: an 800,000-tonne locked, country-specific, licence-administered UK tranche within a 1,000,000-tonne pool (an 80% UK share protected in legal text from dilution by the separate Turkey, Korea, India and Japan processes), a 35% out-of-quota bound rate, six-year duration, and a year-three trigger-based review (objective pre-defined triggers, mutual agreement, 20% cap, single exercise, cap review at year five). The package secures every EU objective: the restraint commitment in the UK's own drafted language covering the real systemic risk of UK participation in a Japan/Korea dispute track; a bankable three-year standstill on EU country-specific access under the UK steel measure with transparency and advance consultation; TCA preferences preserved only within the tranche with all UK preferential access counting against it; and the FTA disapplication maintained in force outside the tranche, exposed only to review-scoped remedies flowing through the same trigger and cap architecture. The UK's final-round move of 650,000 tonnes (1.8M to 1.15M) and its request to confirm finality are pre-acceptance positioning, not rejection; there is no authority and no justification to move beyond 800,000 or below 35%, and doing so would be negotiating against ourselves while undercutting our stated floors with the other claimants we must still settle. Accepting now puts a single, unambiguous set of terms before London in the same round, maximising the chance of convergence and a June Council vote. If London declines, we proceed as notified having demonstrably offered double the notified quota with structural protections — the strongest possible record for the Trade Policy Committee, member states, and any subsequent dispute or retaliation debate, with the option to revisit these structural elements before any UK withdrawal of concessions takes effect.

Ministers have decided to accept the EU's final package, superseding the 850,000-tonne floor and 30% ceiling. The package — an 800,000-tonne locked UK tranche (80% share) within a 1,000,000-tonne pool, country-specific licence-administered allocation on a recent-reference basis, protected in operative legal text from dilution by the Turkey/Korea/India/Japan processes, TCA preferences preserved inside the tranche, a 35% out-of-quota bound rate, a year-three review with objective triggers and a 20% adjustment cap, FTA disapplication brought within the review with a presumption of remedy, our narrow restraint formulation accepted as drafted, the three-year safeguard standstill, and valued compensation engagement — is materially better on every dimension than the notified default (400,000 tonnes global first-come-first-served at 50% with no lock, no TCA preservation and no review). The structural concessions won across four rounds would be lost entirely in a no-deal, and the six-month retaliation route could not recover equivalent value for an industry facing existential pressure. Acceptance is recorded with three conditions for the legal text: the anti-dilution lock in operative language, trigger definitions capable of qualifying under current depressed market conditions so the review can move the tranche upward, and melt-and-pour/licensing per standing parameters (standard certification, automatic licensing, quota-fill monitoring with reallocation of unused capacity), alongside a drafting timetable ahead of the June Council vote.
